blocks.content: If you have ever watched a pandas script crawl through a million rows, there is a good chance df.iterrows() was the culprit. It feels natural — loop over rows, do something, move on. But iterrows() is one of the slowest things you can do in pandas, and there is almost always a better way.

blocks.text: Why is it slow? Each iteration converts the row into a pandas Series, which means dtype checks and Python-level overhead on every single row. You pay that tax a million times. Here are five faster approaches, ordered from fastest to slowest.

blocks.content: Nine times out of ten, you do not need a loop at all. Pandas and NumPy operate on whole columns in compiled C code. If your row logic is arithmetic or comparisons, express it column-wise.

blocks.code:
# Instead of looping: one line, compiled C speed
df['total'] = df['price'] * df['quantity']

# Conditional logic without a loop
df['tier'] = (df['total'] > 1000).map({True: 'premium', False: 'standard'})

blocks.content: When each row needs if/elif/else logic, np.select keeps it vectorized. You describe the conditions once, NumPy applies them to the whole column.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

conditions = [df['total'] > 1000, df['total'] > 100]
choices = ['premium', 'regular']
df['tier'] = np.select(conditions, choices, default='basic')

blocks.text: 3. itertuples — when you truly must loop

blocks.content: Some logic cannot be vectorized — calling an external API per row, for example. In that case, swap iterrows() for itertuples(). It yields lightweight namedtuples instead of Series objects and is dramatically faster, often 10 to 100 times.

blocks.text: 4. Build a list, then assign once

blocks.content: A Python list comprehension over zip() of the underlying NumPy arrays avoids Series construction entirely. Collect results in a list and assign the whole column in one shot.

blocks.code:
# Fast pure-Python loop over raw arrays
totals = [p * q for p, q in zip(df['price'].to_numpy(),
                                df['quantity'].to_numpy())]
df['total'] = totals

blocks.content: df.apply() with axis=1 is still a Python-level loop, so it is slower than vectorization — but it skips the Series-per-row construction cost of iterrows() and reads far cleaner for complex per-row functions.

Vectorize first. Reach for np.where or np.select for branching. If you must loop, use itertuples() or a list comprehension — never iterrows(). Your future self, staring at a progress bar at 2 AM, will thank you.

blocks.text: Fast code is not clever code. It is code that respects where the real cost lives — and in pandas, the cost lives in the loop.

excerpt: df.iterrows() is one of the slowest things you can do in pandas. Here are five faster ways to work row-by-row — from full vectorization to the least-bad loop.
title: Stop Using df.iterrows(): 5 Faster Ways to Work Row-by-Row in Pandas
